title: Commonwealth debt: Interest bill to eclipse Medicare spend by 2029
full_text:
The federal government will soon spend more on interest repayments than on Medicare as a wave of ultra-cheap COVID-era debt rolls onto much higher interest rates, forcing Treasurer Jim Chalmers to confront the rising cost of a budget expected to remain in deficit for decades.
The Commonwealth's already surging debt bill is forecast to rise sharply over the next four years as $165 billion in low-cost debt, borrowed by the Morrison government at rock-bottom rates to prop up the economy during the pandemic, rolls off onto much higher interest rates.
Treasury forecasts that interest payments will overtake Medicare spending by 2028-29, when servicing the forecast $1.2 trillion federal debt will cost $41.9 billion a year - almost $2 billion more than projected spending on medical benefits.
"The way to think about the COVID debt was that we stopped the economy from going into a deep recession, and that was the pay-off," said former RBA board member Warwick McKibbin.
"But the cost of that - instead of it happening up front - it's going to be spread out over many years. Our strategy should be to finance that by running small surpluses ... which we're clearly not."
The pandemic-era debt currently carries an average interest rate of just 0.5 per cent, costing taxpayers a modest $800 million a year. But refinancing the $165 billion debt at rates above 5 per cent will push the annual interest bill to $8.5 billion - a $7.7 billion hit to the budget each year, according to estimates from Barrenjoey.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealed this week that the mid-year budget update, due by December, would show surging global interest rates had led to a multi-billion-dollar blowout in the government's interest bill, which was already forecast to cost $146.3 billion over the next four years.
"If you read the international economic commentary, the biggest thing that's going on right now is the way that bond yields - which are essentially a reflection of borrowing costs - are going up around the world and quite substantially. And here in Australia as well," Chalmers told The Conversation in a podcast.
With the unemployment rate still a low 4.6 per cent, McKibbin said the federal government was in the stage of the economic cycle where it should be running a budget surplus and paying down debt.
Instead, the Albanese government expects to record a $64.1 billion headline budget deficit this financial year. The figure includes so-called "off budget" spending on items like the $15 billion National Reconstruction Fund to diversify industry and the $10 billion Housing Australia Future Fund for new social and affordable homes.
"The original Charter of Budget Honesty was a good idea under [Liberal treasurer] Peter Costello ... but the guardrails have been completely undermined by both governments since the Howard years, by moving a lot of items off budget," McKibbin said.
"I think there definitely needs to be some fiscal rules put back in place so you can constrain this sort of very large fiscal spending that we're seeing now."
Bond yields have soared globally to multi-decade highs this year because of growing concerns about the sustainability of government budgets - particularly in the United States - and fears the conflict in the Middle East will keep oil prices and inflation elevated.
Sovereign governments such as Australia seeking to raise money on bond markets now also have to compete with US technology giants, which are issuing hundreds of billions in debt to fund the artificial intelligence boom.
Australia's 10-year bond yield now stands at 5.4 per cent, up from about 4.8 per cent at the start of the year and 5 per cent in May.
The sharp rise in borrowing costs was not factored into recent federal or state budgets, which assumed interest rates would remain around the average levels prevailing when they were prepared - about half of one percentage point below current levels.
The Australian Financial Review reported last week that the rise in yields since May would add about $6 billion to the budget deficit over the next four financial years, according to an estimate from RBC Capital Markets.
McKibbin said extra debt was not necessarily problematic if it was used for productive assets such as infrastructure. But if used to pay for day-to-day government spending - as he believes it to be now - then it would need to be paid for with future taxes.
"It's not free. You've got to pay for it out of something, and probably out of more taxes. And the question is, how much damage do those taxes do," McKibbin said.
